# What Happens When People Are Randomly Given the Opportunity to Obtain Medicaid?
# DUE OCT 19TH

In 2008, Oregon had money to expand Medicaid coverage, but not enough money to cover everyone who wanted it. The state used a lottery to select some people from a waiting list. This created an unusual opportunity to study the effects of expanding access to public health insurance using a randomized design.

But what exactly was randomized? The treatment was **winning the opportunity to apply for Medicaid**. Winning the lottery did not guarantee that a person would apply, remain eligible, or obtain coverage.

Recall that problem sets are graded by completion. I want you to try to figure things out on your own, with friends, or with help from me or Alex. The point is to understand what the code is doing and what the results mean.

HINT: Nothing here is intentionally tricky. Sessions 13 and 14 contain every code snippet you need.

You can also now use AI to help you.  But use it to help, don't outsource your thinking and agency to a machine.  If you want to be capable you need to be able to work _with_ AI. 

Fill in the answers in the spots below. Test things out using `Run Current Chunk` and then, when everything works, `Knit` from above - `Knit to PDF` is best. Make sure you save the name of this file to contain your VUNET ID!  

NOTE: if it is not compiling for you send the document to AI and ask it to help you debug it! Figure out what went wrong and then go ahead.   

The questions are in *italics*. Put your written answers after each question and your code in the answer chunk. When I ask what you observe, tell me what the number means!

## The data

Keep this Rmd and `oregon.csv` in the same folder.

Each row is an adult in a single-family household who signed up **alone** for the 2008 lottery. The lottery information and Medicaid enrollment come from state records and exist for everyone. The other outcomes come from a mail survey about a year later and from in-person interviews about two years later, so they exist only for the people who took part; everyone else is `NA`.

| Variable | Meaning |
|:--|:--|
| `lottery` | `"Selected"` or `"Not selected"` in the 2008 lottery. |
| `female`, `age`, `english` | Recorded when the person signed up, before the lottery. `age` is age in 2008; `english` = 1 if they asked for English-language materials. |
| `medicaid` | 1 = ever enrolled in Medicaid between March 2008 and September 2009 (state records); 0 = never. |
| `survey` | 1 = returned the twelve-month mail survey; 0 = did not. The variables below through `depressed` are `NA` unless `survey` is 1. |
| `rx`, `doctor`, `er`, `hospital` | 1 = any prescription drug use, any doctor visit, any ER visit, any hospital stay in the last six months. |
| `oop`, `owe`, `borrowed` | 1 = any out-of-pocket medical spending; currently owe money for medical care; borrowed money or skipped bills to pay medical bills. |
| `health_good` | 1 = rates own health good, very good, or excellent; 0 = fair or poor. |
| `days_physical_bad`, `days_mental_bad` | Days out of the last 30 when physical (mental) health was not good. |
| `depressed` | 1 = screened positive for depression on a two-question screener. |
| `inperson` | 1 = interviewed in person in the Portland area, 2009–2010. The three variables below are `NA` unless `inperson` is 1. |
| `bp_systolic`, `cholesterol`, `a1c` | Blood pressure (mm Hg), total cholesterol (mg/dl), and hemoglobin A1c (percent), measured at the interview. |
| `VotedSim2008`, `VotedSim2010` | 1 = voted in the November 2008 (2010) election. **These two columns are simulated.** See the note at the end. |

NOTE: `VotedSim2008` and `VotedSim2010` are not real voting records. The actual study uses Oregon voter files. These columns were generated to reproduce that study's published results.

## Where the data came from

The Oregon Health Insurance Experiment public-use data: Finkelstein, Amy. 2013. *Oregon Health Insurance Experiment Public Use Data.* National Bureau of Economic Research and Harvard Dataverse. <https://doi.org/10.7910/DVN/SJG1ED>. `oregon.csv` keeps people who signed up for the lottery alone and a small set of variables from the descriptive, state-program, twelve-month mail survey, and in-person interview files. No weights are used.

Published studies these data come from:

- Finkelstein, Amy, et al. 2012. "The Oregon Health Insurance Experiment: Evidence from the First Year." *Quarterly Journal of Economics* 127(3): 1057–1106. <https://doi.org/10.1093/qje/qjs020>.
- Baicker, Katherine, et al. 2013. "The Oregon Experiment—Effects of Medicaid on Clinical Outcomes." *New England Journal of Medicine* 368: 1713–1722. <https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMsa1212321>.
- Baicker, Katherine, and Amy Finkelstein. 2019. "The Impact of Medicaid Expansion on Voter Participation: Evidence from the Oregon Health Insurance Experiment." *Quarterly Journal of Political Science* 14(4): 383–400. <https://doi.org/10.1561/100.00019026>. [PDF](BaickerFinkelstein_2019_MedicaidVoterParticipation_QJPS.pdf).

**About `VotedSim2008` and `VotedSim2010`.** The voting study matched the lottery list to Oregon voter files that are not public. These two columns were simulated for this assignment so that the lottery groups reproduce that study's published turnout rates and effects, overall and by gender, with no effect in 2010. They are not measurements of any real person's voting.
